headline: Tuesday night's storm trended weaker today: GFS dropped its burst, and the remaining models bring mostly steady light rain Tuesday evening into Wednesday morning, peaking near the 7.1 ft high tide around 1 AM Wednesday, well below flooding amounts.

summary.text: GFS, this morning's wet outlier, fell from 0.49 to 0.10 in for its wettest 3 hours. Consensus barely moved (0.11 to 0.14 in). NWS also says the storm is trending less impactful.
Wettest 3 hours, next 72 h: RRFS 0.30, ECMWF 0.20, NBM 0.14, GFS 0.10, HRRR 0.00 in (HRRR ends 10 AM Tuesday). RRFS is now the wettest, with a 0.14 in hour at 1 AM Wednesday.
No street flooding expected on the consensus (0.14 in). Yellow (garage) needs about 0.71 in in 3 hours or a 0.40 in hour; no model has an hour above 0.14 in.
Dry tonight and Monday. Light rain starts about 5 PM Tuesday; RRFS and NBM are heaviest 11 PM Tuesday to 2 AM Wednesday, ECMWF later, 5 to 8 AM Wednesday. Drying Wednesday afternoon.
Tides running about 1.3 to 1.4 ft above prediction at high tide. The RRFS/NBM peak overlaps the 7.1 ft high at 1:12 AM Wednesday. Channel low and steady: 0.14 ft at Alameda.
Use dry Monday to clear street drain grates and yard drains and check sandbags. Keep the page open Tuesday evening in case a thunderstorm cell forms on the front.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: Post-frontal showers are fading this afternoon and should end overnight; NWS San Francisco (12:16 PM) calls Monday a mainly dry break and recommends using it to clear storm drains and gutters. The next upper trough and cold front arrive Tuesday into Wednesday. NWS notes a continuing trend toward a less impactful system: the American and European models now bring the moisture plume in at a steeper angle, pulling the heaviest rain offshore and leaving a gap between moisture pulses. NWS rain totals: 0.25 to 1 inch across the Bay Area (more toward the coast), gusts 20 to 30 mph, and a slight chance of thunderstorms with the main frontal band, where locally heavy downpours could develop. Thanksgiving looks dry; another, more uncertain storm is possible late Friday into the weekend. Separately, NWS expects major to extreme coastal flooding around the high tides all week.

sections.title: What changed and model trends
sections.text:
Since this morning's discussion the burst that GFS showed for early Wednesday is gone, and the other models nudged slightly. Wettest 3 hours / total, 4 PM Sunday to 4 PM Wednesday:
• RRFS (10 AM Sun run, reaches Wednesday night): 0.30 / 0.46 in, wettest 11 PM Tuesday to 2 AM Wednesday, with 0.12 in at midnight and 0.14 in at 1 AM. This morning: 0.26 in, peaking at 2 AM. Essentially unchanged, about an hour earlier.
• ECMWF: 0.20 / 0.30 in, up from 0.14 in, but later: nearly dry Tuesday, wettest 5 to 8 AM Wednesday (0.07 in per hour).
• NBM: 0.14 / 0.52 in, up from 0.11 in. Steady 0.035 to 0.05 in per hour from 5 PM Tuesday to 5 AM Wednesday, wettest 11 PM to 2 AM.
• GFS: 0.10 / 0.12 in, down from 0.49 / 0.55 in. One 0.08 in hour at 9 PM Tuesday and almost nothing Wednesday.
• HRRR (2 PM Sun run): 0.00 in. It ends at 10 AM Tuesday, before the rain; its 15-minute output is dry through Monday night.

Consensus (HRRR 0.00 × 1.25, RRFS 0.30, NBM 0.14): 0.14 in, up slightly from 0.11 in. With HRRR not yet reaching the storm, that middle value comes from RRFS and NBM; the middle of RRFS, ECMWF and NBM would be 0.20 in. Either way it stays far under the 0.71 in Yellow threshold, and the largest single hour in any model (0.14 in) is about a third of the 0.40 in one-hour burst level. The caveat: HRRR-type guidance has under-forecast local bursts by about 3× before, and NWS keeps a slight chance of thunderstorms on the front, which models handle poorly.

sections.title: Tide and the channel
sections.text:
NOAA's Bay model runs about 1.3 to 1.4 ft above the predicted high tides at Redwood City (about 1.2 ft at this afternoon's low). Tonight's 6.9 ft high at 11:18 PM runs about 8.3 ft; Monday's 9.2 ft high at 10:20 AM about 10.6 ft; Monday night's 7.0 ft high at 12:16 AM Tuesday about 8.4 ft; Tuesday's 9.5 ft high at 11:02 AM about 10.8 ft. The model now ends at 1 PM Tuesday, so the storm itself is predictions only: a -1.5 ft low at 6:28 PM Tuesday (good drainage as the rain starts), 7.1 ft at 1:12 AM Wednesday, 3.2 ft low at 6:14 AM, and the 9.5 ft king tide at 11:46 AM Wednesday. The RRFS/NBM peak falls right around the 1:12 AM high, which with surge slows the channel; ECMWF's later peak falls on the falling tide toward the 6:14 AM low, which drains better. By the late-morning king tide Wednesday, all models have the rain nearly over.

NWS coastal products are unchanged: Coastal Flood Advisory until 6 AM Monday, then a Coastal Flood Warning through 4 PM Thursday. San Francisco high tides 2.2 ft above normal Monday, 2.6 Tuesday, 2.8 Wednesday and 2.4 Thursday, including up to 1.6 ft of surge.

Channel: at Alameda de las Pulgas it reads 0.14 ft at 4 PM, flat all day (Flood Monitoring 3.18 ft). The gauge upstream of Caltrain last reported 0.07 ft at 5:13 AM Sunday (Flood Monitoring 2.8 ft), about 11 hours ago.

sections.title: Current observations
sections.text: Dry on the street this afternoon. The Caltrain rain gauge showed 0.04 in over the 24 hours ending at its last report, 5:13 AM Sunday, all from last night's front. The Alameda channel gauge has held between 0.13 and 0.17 ft all day. NWS reports showers only over the Central Coast and southern and eastern Santa Clara County, decreasing this evening.

sections.title: Uncertainty
sections.text: Low through Monday night: no model has rain. Moderate for Tuesday night into Wednesday: all four models that reach it bring rain, now in a tighter range (wettest 3 hours 0.10 to 0.30 in), with the wet GFS solution dropped and NWS describing a weakening trend. The main open questions are timing (RRFS and NBM near the 1 AM high tide vs ECMWF around dawn) and whether a thunderstorm forms on the frontal band, which could give a short downpour heavier than any model shows. HRRR will begin covering Tuesday night with its runs late tonight and Monday.

sections.title: What to do
sections.text:
• Nothing needed tonight.
• Monday (dry): clear leaves from street drain grates and yard drains, check sandbags, and decide where cars go Tuesday night if the forecast trends wetter. Tuesday's wind gusts can cause power outages, which slow the pumps.
• Tuesday evening: keep this page open; if a downpour develops, timestamped photos at the peak help.
• Stay away from the Bay shore and tidal sloughs at the late-morning high tides all week; don't walk or drive through moving water.
